pulls.title: mining: move getblocktemplate cache into BlockTemplateManager
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #35675. This addresses the `getblocktemplate` part of the "Remove remaining global states" TODO in #33758, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35675#pullrequestreview-5299625960.

`getblocktemplate` reuses its last template until the tip changes, or until the mempool changes and the template is more than 5 seconds old. That cache currently lives in four function-local statics, which:

- live as long as the process, so the cached `CBlockIndex*` can outlive its `ChainstateManager` (as in unit tests);
- rely on `cs_main` being held, which nothing checks;
- can't be unit tested.

This PR moves the cache into `BlockTemplateManager`, in three commits:

1. **rpc:** refactors the statics in place into a `CachedBlockTemplate` struct and a `GetNewOrCachedBlockTemplate()` helper, `GUARDED_BY(::cs_main)`. The template's `hashPrevBlock` replaces the cached `CBlockIndex*`, and the 5 seconds becomes `GBT_TEMPLATE_REBUILD_INTERVAL`.
2. **refactor:** moves them into `BlockTemplateManager`. It's easiest to review with `git show --color-moved=dimmed-zebra --color-moved-ws=allow-indentation-change`.
3. **test:** adds a unit test for each rebuild rule and for the retry after a failed build.

No behavior change is intended, and only `getblocktemplate` uses the cache. It uses `cs_main` rather than its own mutex, since the RPC already holds it and building a template takes it anyway.

pulls.title: mining: move BlockAssembler statics into BlockTemplateManager
pulls.body:
Based on https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36356. Together with it, this completes the "Remove remaining global states" TODO in #33758.

`getmininginfo` reports `currentblockweight` and `currentblocktx` from two process-wide statics, `BlockAssembler::m_last_block_weight` and `m_last_block_num_txs`, which every `BlockAssembler::CreateNewBlock()` call overwrites. 

Like the `getblocktemplate` statics, they are shared by every node context in the process and nothing checks their locking. They also record templates that were not built for mining: the mempool fee estimator builds its own templates with `BlockAssembler`, so `getmininginfo` can report the fee estimator's template instead of the last mining template.

This PR:

- makes the two fields per-`BlockAssembler` instance, still set at the same point in `CreateNewBlock()`;
- has `BlockTemplateManager::CreateNewTemplate()` record them in a member guarded by `cs_main`, which `getmininginfo` reads. `CreateNewTemplate()` now holds `cs_main` across the build, as `CreateNewBlock()` already did internally, so concurrent builds cannot record their stats out of order;
- adds a unit test showing that manager builds are recorded, that the latest one wins, and that a direct `BlockAssembler` build is ignored.

In short: the last global mining state moves out of `BlockAssembler`, and `getmininginfo` reports the last template built for mining rather than whatever the node assembled last.

pulls.title: net: limit relative ban times to uint32
pulls.body:
`BanMan::Ban` computes the ban end as `GetTime() + bantime` (banman.cpp:140). `setban` and `-bantime` both accept any int64, so a relative bantime close to `INT64_MAX`:

```
setban 1.2.3.5 add 9223372036854775807
```

returns success, but the sum overflows. UBSan reports:

```
src/banman.cpp:140:73: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 1790412558 + 9223372036854775807 cannot be represented in type 'int64_t'
```

Without UBSan the result wraps negative, the ban is treated as already expired, and it is silently dropped. With `-bantime=9223372036854775807` the same happens to every `setban add` that uses the default duration.

This limits relative ban times to uint32 (about 136 years):

- `setban` rejects a relative bantime above `UINT32_MAX` with "Error: bantime is too large"
- `-bantime` is parsed as `uint32_t`, so larger values saturate at `UINT32_MAX`

Absolute timestamps are unchanged.

The added cases in `rpc_setban.py` check that `UINT32_MAX + 1` and `INT64_MAX` are rejected, that `UINT32_MAX` is accepted, and that with `-bantime=INT64_MAX` a default-duration ban is listed with a duration of `UINT32_MAX`. Both parts fail on master and pass with the change. `p2p_disconnect_ban.py` still passes.

AI tools were used to help find this issue and to prepare the patch and test.

pulls.title: mempool: keep prioritisetransaction deltas within MAX_MONEY
pulls.body:
`prioritisetransaction` takes `fee_delta` as any int64. `CTxMemPool::PrioritiseTransaction` stacks deltas with `SaturatingAdd`, so the accumulated delta and the modified fee can go up to `INT64_MAX`. The cluster mempool then adds modified fees of several transactions together in `FeeFrac` (util/feefrac.h:108) without overflow checks.

For example, with a parent and child in the mempool:

```
prioritisetransaction <parent> 0 4611686018427387904
prioritisetransaction <child> 0 9223372036854775807
```

- `getmempoolcluster` reports `chunkfee: -46116860184.27356705`
- `getblocktemplate` contains neither transaction, and the next block mined has only the coinbase
- UBSan: `feefrac.h:108:13: runtime error: signed integer overflow`, reached from linearization via `getrawmempool`

There's no use for a delta larger than the total money supply, so this:

- rejects `fee_delta` outside `-MAX_MONEY..MAX_MONEY` in the RPC with "fee_delta out of range"
- clamps the accumulated delta to `-MAX_MONEY..MAX_MONEY` in `PrioritiseTransaction`, which also covers deltas loaded from mempool.dat, and updates the modified fee by the change in the clamped delta

With each modified fee bounded by 2 * MAX_MONEY, cluster sums stay far away from int64 limits.

The new `test_fee_delta_limits` in `mining_prioritisetransaction.py` checks the RPC range error, that stacked deltas stop at `MAX_MONEY`, that the chunk fees add up, and that both transactions are in the block template. It fails on master ("No exception raised"). `mempool_persist.py`, `mempool_packages.py`, `rpc_packages.py` and the miner/rbf/txpackage unit tests pass.

AI tools were used to help find this issue and to prepare the patch and test.

pulls.title: mempool: recalculate stale BIP68 lockpoints in removeForReorg
pulls.body:
When a reorg lowers the tip, `removeForReorg` can evict BIP68 transactions that are still valid at the new tip, together with all their descendants.

A transaction that spends an unconfirmed parent gets its lockpoints cached with that input at height tip+1. After `invalidateblock`, `TestLockPointValidity` can still pass on those cached lockpoints (always when every input was unconfirmed, since `maxInputBlock` is then genesis; and with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs when the confirmed input's block survives), so `CheckSequenceLocksAtTip` is evaluated against stale values and the transaction is removed.

The fix, suggested by ismaelsadeeq, is to never evict on cached lockpoints alone: if they are not valid at the new tip, or the cached sequence-lock check fails, recalculate them with `CalculateLockPointsAtTip` and evict only if the fresh result also fails. This covers height-based and time-based locks alike, at the cost of some recalculations that turn out to be unnecessary.

test_reorg_stale_lockpoints() in feature_bip68_sequence.py covers four cases across a reorg: a BIP68-disabled child, a BIP68-enabled child of an unconfirmed parent, a child with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs, and a time-based zero lock where the reorg lowers the median time past (test by Bicaru20). The test fails on master, and the mixed-input case also fails on the earlier genesis-only version of this fix.

test_reorg_unsatisfied_lock_evicted() (by instagibbs) is the counterpart: it checks that transactions whose relative lock is genuinely unsatisfied after the reorg are still evicted, together with their descendants.

Reproducer for unpatched nodes:
https://gist.github.com/javierpmateos/c55d365973adbf488a852dc5e0b77dec

Same class of issue fixed for TRUC in #33504.

Closes #35007

pulls.title: node: don't abort on invalid -dbcache in settings.json
pulls.body:
`LogOversizedDbCache` (added in #33333) is `noexcept`, but it reads `-dbcache` through `CalculateDbCacheBytes` -> `GetIntArg`. `GetIntArg` throws when settings.json has a number that isn't an integer or doesn't fit in int64, e.g. `{"dbcache": 4096.5}`. The exception hits the `noexcept` boundary and bitcoind aborts during startup:

```
libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::runtime_error: JSON integer out of range
```

This removes `noexcept`. The exception now reaches the handler in `AppInit`, and the node exits with status 1 and an error message instead of aborting:

```
EXCEPTION: St13runtime_error
JSON integer out of range
bitcoin in AppInit()
```

The added case in `feature_settings.py` writes `{"dbcache": 4096.5}` to settings.json and checks that startup fails with that message from `AppInit`.

pulls.title: p2p: replace full outbound peers that don't support tx relay (take 2)
pulls.body:
Picks up #28538

Outbound-full-relay slots should be used by peers that actually relay transactions, besides #28538 see #16418 and #28371 for the motivation. So try to replace peers that are not relaying txs with peers that do.

The approach differs from the original PR in a few details in response to some of the review comments there:

- A replacement is connected before the peer is evicted. The original PR disconnected a non-tx-relaying peer once all full outbound slots were filled. Reviewers preferred having a replacement available first (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). Now an extra outbound-full-relay connection is requested, like the extra network-specific peers, and the existing eviction of extra outbound peers prefers peers that don't relay txs.
- Peers not relaying txs don't get `m_protect`. Otherwise they could stay forever (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443336121), and ignoring the protection was rejected in the same thread (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443312604).
- An only peer on a network is not replaced. Otherwise the network-specific extra connections and this logic would keep replacing each other (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). This also covers the `-maxconnections=1` case (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1417178196).

Nothing is changed in `-blocksonly` mode or during IBD. The rename commit and the functional test are taken from the original PR with some changes to match the new behavior.

pulls.title: test: Fix intermittent issue in p2p_orphan_handling.py
pulls.body:
Turns out https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32092 was incomplete and the issue can still happen:

https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/39809026827/job/119929911875#step:14:14454

The basic idea is that peer1 disconnects to clear its orphan state. This happens in `DisconnectNodes`->`DeleteNode`->`FinalizeNode`->`TxDownloadManager::DisconnectedPeer`.

In my prior fix, I assumed that `DisconnectNodes` in the `net` thread would be possible to sync on via a ping-pong. However, the msghand thread may hold a reference to the node, preventing deletion and only moving the node to `m_nodes_disconnected`. Afterward, the `net` thread may hand the pings to the `msghand` thread and go to sleep for a bit.

Thus, the test proceed and cause a split `getdata`, meaning that `peer2.wait_for_parent_requests([int(parent_peekaboo_AB["txid"], 16), int(parent_missing["txid"], 16)])` fails.

Fix this by just waiting for `TxDownloadManager::DisconnectedPeer` to have happened via `self.wait_until(lambda: len(node.getorphantxs(verbosity=2)[0]["from"]) == 1)`.


Edit: Possible diff to reproduce with ~10% failure rate:

```diff
diff --git a/src/net.cpp b/src/net.cpp
index 1201d3bcb4..e81623484b 100644
```

pulls.title: wallet: fix migration of watch-only wallets with transactions
pulls.body:
Migrating a legacy wallet that holds no spendable material fails whenever the
wallet contains transactions. `migratewallet` returns
`std::bad_function_call (-1)` and the wallet is left unmigrated.

Two defects are involved, and the first one hides the second.

### 1. The migration check reads in-memory state that has not been updated yet

When the wallet being migrated has no spendable material,
`CWallet::ApplyMigrationData()` asserts that nothing is left behind in it:

```cpp
if (!m_address_book.empty()) return util::Error{_("Error: Not all address book records were migrated")};
if (!mapWallet.empty()) return util::Error{_("Error: Not all transaction records were migrated")};
```

The two checks look symmetric but are not. `DelAddressBookWithDB()` erases from
`m_address_book` straight away, so the first check sees current state.
`RemoveTxs()` only erases the transaction records from disk; it defers the
`mapWallet` removal to the db txn's `on_commit` listener, which does not run
until the txn is committed — after `ApplyMigrationData()` has returned.

`mapWallet` is therefore never empty at that point and the check always fails.

### 2. Aborting the txn calls a callback that was never set

`DbTxnListener` declares `on_commit` and `on_abort` as plain `std::function`
members and callers may set only the one they need. `RemoveTxs()` does exactly
that: `on_commit` is set, `on_abort` is left empty.

`TxnCommit()` and `TxnAbort()` each invoked their listener's callback
unconditionally, so the abort triggered by the failed check above threw
`std::bad_function_call`. The exception escaped the wallet entirely, replacing
the real error with an unhelpful one and skipping the caller's cleanup path.

### Fix

The first commit skips callbacks that are not set, and documents that they are
optional. The second discounts the transactions already queued for deletion
instead of requiring `mapWallet` to be empty.

They are kept separate because the second defect masks the first: with only the
listener fix applied, the migration surfaces the real error
`Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)` instead of
`std::bad_function_call (-1)`.

### Testing

`src/wallet/test/db_tests.cpp` gains a regression test covering a listener with
only one callback set, for both commit and abort. It fails on master with
`std::bad_function_call` and passes with the fix.

`test/functional/wallet_migration.py` gains a case migrating a blank legacy
wallet with a watch-only address that has received a transaction. The test is
taken from #36483.

To reproduce on master, apply the functional test alone and run
`wallet_migration.py`.

Fixes #36483

pulls.title: fuzz: check GetStale() returns exactly the stale private broadcast txs
pulls.body:
The `private_broadcast` fuzz test checks each tx that `GetStale()` returns. This adds to it by checking that all stale txs are returned.  `ReattemptPrivateBroadcast()` only retries what `GetStale()` returns, and a stale tx left out is never retried.

This partly came up during review in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35129#pullrequestreview-4427536924, and recently also surfaced in https://mutanthub.space/mutants/3752 , where changing `continue` to `break` in `GetStale()` passes all current tests.

This PR records when each tx is added and when each node confirms it. Then it checks that `GetStale()` returns exactly the expected txs.

pulls.title: qa: check more socket API invariants for each platform we support
pulls.body:
This improves our `Sock` test coverage following CVE-2026-117350.

This leaves out the test for the specific case that led to the OOM until we [fix `select()` reporting](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36688#issue-6085527087) for urgent data, but i'm also trying not to fight the last battle too much. Instead i focused on trying to pin down all invariants Claude and I could come up with that could be reasonably tested. This will help us understand our code better, and get more assurance we do not break some assumption a (security critical) caller may be relying on further down the road.

Another goal is to tie the events our fuzzing mock can report to the events each OS actually reports, and when. A follow-up will extend the mock to match what these tests pin down. This wouldn’t have caught the CVE-2026-117350 bug: it was in the very logic the mock replaces, so a fuzz target could only have found it if the mock had been written with that bug in mind. But the next bug may well be somewhere else, and a mock that can report everything the real socket APIs can, lets the fuzzer reach corner cases which may lack a proper unit test.

A lot more coverage could be added. I chose not to add tests specific to the logic used for trusted interfaces (Tor control, the SOCKS5 proxy, I2P SAM) or to a single platform. I also left out the test which led me to find https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36688#issuecomment-6509375262, as this needs to be fixed first.

pulls.title: init: refuse -bytespersigop values that overflow
pulls.body:
`-bytespersigop` is parsed as int64, stored as unsigned int, and multiplied by a transaction's sigop cost into the int32 sizes used by the mempool. Negative values wrap, values of 2^32 or more are truncated (4294967296 turns the sigop adjustment off), and large values overflow, so a debug build aborts on an `Assume`. The first commit refuses any value outside [0, 21474] at startup: up to 21474, a package of 25 transactions at the standard sigops limit still has an int32 size.

The second commit checks the sigops limit before a transaction is staged. A transaction that is otherwise standard can be far over that limit, and at 21474 one with about 100,000 sigops still overflows when staged. `mempool_sigoplimit.py` covers the range, a 25-transaction package at 21474, and that transaction.

pulls.title: rpc: Use self.Arg<_>(name) helper over manual and duplicate parsing
pulls.body:
The `Arg()` helper has many benefits:

* It does not require manual `isNull` checks
* It does not require hard-coding the fallback/default value a second time
* It does not require manually specifying the getter for the type. Specifying the type is enough.

So use it more broadly.

pulls.title: rpc: Report -rpcwhitelist denials as JSON-RPC errors
pulls.body:
This PR adds two JSON-RPC error codes for requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist`, which until now got an HTTP 403 status with an empty body:

- `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` (-38) is returned for a refused request, with HTTP 200 for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and 403 for legacy 1.x requests.
- `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` (-39) is returned for the other requests in a refused batch. A refused batch now gets HTTP 200 and an array with an error for each request, and still runs none of them.

**Problem:** `-rpcwhitelist` errors are currently handled differently from other JSON-RPC errors, so clients report them with vague or misleading messages, and for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests the handling does not follow [documented behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md#json-rpc-11-vs-20). Specifically, requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist` get HTTP 403 with an empty body, so the refusal shows up as a generic transport error rather than a specific JSON-RPC error. This is especially a problem for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, which are [supposed to](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/bf1a1f1662427fbf1a43bb951364eface469bdb7) report failed method calls only as JSON-RPC errors, not HTTP errors. The empty reply causes a concrete problem when JSON-RPC requests are sent over IPC instead of HTTP: `bitcoin-cli -ipcconnect` receives only the response body, so a refused call prints a JSON type error instead of a permission error, as described in a [private security review](https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/audits/ar-56/). Over HTTP, `bitcoin-cli` currently stops at the 403 status and prints only "server returned HTTP error 403" instead of the actual error.

**Solution:** Report whitelist denials like any other failed call: a JSON-RPC error in the body, with the HTTP status the request's version calls for. This brings the behavior in line with the documentation. `bitcoin-cli` then prints the permission error over both HTTP and IPC, with no change to the IPC interface. Small change to `src/httprpc.cpp` and `src/rpc/protocol.h`, with tests in `rpc_whitelist.py` and `interface_ipc_cli.py`. Details in the commit messages.

Compatibility: HTTP clients that send `"jsonrpc": "2.0"` or batches and check for a 403 status need to read the error code instead. Single 1.x requests keep the 403 status, now with an error body.

Open question for review: `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` could be named `RPC_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` is documented as batch-specific but would fit any request refused before it runs.

pulls.title: init: don't wrap the default onion port to 0 for -port=65535
pulls.body:
The default onion port is `-port` + 1, computed in `uint16_t`. With `-port=65535` it wrapped to 0, so the default onion listener bound to `127.0.0.1:0` (an ephemeral port nobody can reach) and the same port 0 was used for `-bind=<addr>=onion` without a port and as the onion service target.

Fail at startup with an error that asks for a lower `-port` or an explicit onion port instead. `-bind=<addr>:<port>=onion` with an explicit port keeps working.

feature_port.py gets a case for both paths; it fails on master (the node starts and binds port 0).

This patch was prepared with AI assistance (Claude) and reviewed and tested by me.

pulls.title: compressor: oversized script decoding can leave a spendable script
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The oversized-script fallback appends `OP_RETURN` to the destination instead of replacing it. If the destination already contains an unfinished push, the appended byte becomes pushed data and the result can remain spendable.

**Fix:** Replace the destination with `OP_RETURN` rather than appending it.

Found while reviewing #36280. This predates that PR and appears latent because oversized outputs are excluded from the UTXO set, but it could affect malformed stored records decoded into a reused destination.

pulls.title: refactor: Use u64 consistently for flatfile sizes
pulls.body:
`unsigned` is a 32-bit integer (even on 64-bit platforms). File sizes are generally measured in 64-bit integers and using 32-bit integers or architecture-dependent integers is brittle and confusing.

So use u64 consistently for flatfile sizes in this refactor.

Also, use `LARGE_INTEGER`'s `QuadPart` on Windows, which is recommended since C++11.

Also, unit test VarInt overflow errors.

pulls.title: p2p: Reconsider package transactions that are immediately trimmed
pulls.body:
In-master, if a package is entered into mempool at the lowerst chunk feerate, pushing the mempool oversize, this causes that transaction (package) to be trimmed immediately. This is fine and expected, but the returned validation result `TX_MEMPOOL_POLICY` precludes the now-evicted parent from being considered again (i.e. fetched / processed as package) until after another block is found.

This is not a major issue, but would result in unneeded censorship of someone low-balling package feerates.

The already-in-mempool case needs a bit more logic due to the `FeeFailure`'s requirement of package feerate knowledge, so I opted to defer it for now.

Related to finding made by Loupe, and subsequently Red Team.

pulls.title: wallet: only rebroadcast transactions originating from the wallet
pulls.body:
As explained in #3828, rebroadcast of transactions paying the wallet (but not spending any wallet inputs) is a privacy leak, since anyone can generate these, choose a low fee, and observe who rebroadcasts them. 
While it is somewhat intuitive that submitting transactions has privacy implications - at least until confirmation - this is manageable by various strategies (switching to privacy networks for a while, using private broadcast, making sure it confirms before rebroadcast). However, I find it rather unexpected that just passively running a node with a wallet loaded can lead to a loss of privacy as well.

This PR stops rebroadcasting transactions that don't spend any wallet inputs. For the same reason, they are also no longer re-added to the mempool on startup or after an import: otherwise our node might be the only one still having a transaction the rest of the network has dropped, which can be detected with active probing (e.g. by submitting a child).

This does have the trade-off that receivers (who have an incentive to get paid) will now need to manually resubmit transactions if the transaction doesn't confirm and the sender doesn't rebroadcast, but I think it is worth the privacy benefit.

An alternative approach is https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36380, although these could also be combined (make rebroadcast optional, but never rebroadcast non-originating transactions)

Fixes #3828

pulls.title: net, http: always set accepted sockets as non-blocking
pulls.body:
A mistake here would be critical, as it would allow a malicious peer to stall us indefinitely for free. This is not currently an issue because:
- while on Linux accepted sockets do not inherit O_NONBLOCK, we always send() and recv() on Linux/macOS/BSD with MSG_DONTWAIT;
- while on Windows MSG_DONTWAIT is unset, accepted sockets do inherit the non-blocking option [^1].

Therefore, set accepted sockets (inbound P2P connections and HTTP clients) as non-blocking explicitly, like CreateSockOS() does for the sockets it creates. A belt-and-suspenders check costs virtually nothing here, and we already have similar ones for less important options (such as TCP_NODELAY, which as far as i know is inherited by accepted sockets on all our supported platforms).

[^1]: Source is [this](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winsock2/nf-winsock2-accept#remarks) implicit remark in the accept() doc, plus my own testing.

pulls.title: addrman, rpc: classify linked-IPv4 addresses consistently
pulls.body:
Some addresses can be an IPv6 ones with an embedded IPv4 address belongs to. `AddrMan::Size()`, and so the per-network counts in `getaddrmaninfo`, use `GetNetwork()`, which returns ipv6 for these addresses. However, the network filter in `GetAddr_()` and the network / source_network labels in `getnodeaddresses` and `getrawaddrman` use `GetNetClass()`, which returns ipv4 for them.

So on master, for example, for a node whose addrman holds a 6to4 or Teredo address:
  - getaddrmaninfo counts it under ipv6.
  - getnodeaddresses 0 "ipv6" doesn't return it.
  - getnodeaddresses 0 "ipv4" does return it, labelled ipv4.

This PR changes all of this places to use `GetNetwork()`. This way the filter, labels and the counts agree. We should leave `GetNetClass()` usage for netgroup and bucketing decisions, where treating linked-IPv4 addresses as IPv4 is intended. If you pick the change in the fuzz target and run it without the other changes, it's expected to crash to reproduce the issue.

pulls.title: contrib: pass windows codesigning passphrase via stdin
pulls.body:
osslsigncode -pass places the key passphrase in the process arguments, so ps can read it.

So instead, pipe it to -readpass -, which reads it from stdin (osslsigncode 2.9+, the Guix codesign manifest uses 2.14). Since printf is a shell builtin, the passphrase does not appear in any process arguments.

Only sh -n was used to verify, not actual signing keys. This focuses on the Windows part of #36651.

pulls.title: RFC: consensus: Make `CAmount` a class
pulls.body:
We should treat people's money with care across node and wallet.

Having our `CAmount` be a `typedef` for raw `int64_t` as on master has the following drawbacks:
* Allows assigning to from `bool`s, leading to the issues like the one previously fixed by 0026b330c4abbbbdb96e4f0c4d380d70d8e592ab.
* Allows direct comparison with integral types of differing size, leading to things like the issue previously fixed by 890a09b1e49925315a5636f29cc5af36928fe092 (reverting it on top of this PR leads to compile errors).
* Allows forgetting to initialize amounts (`CAmount fee;`).
* Allows direct operations with imprecise decimal types as in `CAmount target = 49.5L * COIN` in src/wallet/test/coinselector_tests.cpp.
* Allows *multiplying* two `CAmount`s with each other, which does not make sense.

Beyond fixing the above, this PR also makes amounts stick out more in code - either by the `CAmount` type itself or by using the `sats` unit specifier.

This work is also a stepping stone for possible future work introducing an even safer amount type which only allows values in the range `[0, MAX_MONEY]`.

Already merged PRs spawned out of this work: #35456, #35372

Prior attempts in similar directions: #5430, #4067
